title: Months needed to review death in custody
article: The investigation into why a drug user died while in police custody will take months to complete, according to the Calgary Police Service.
Tamer Sayed Roha died shortly after police arrived at the Quality Inn on Banff Trail N.W. on Sept. 4.
Officers were responding to reports from motel staff that the 27- year-old man was behaving in a "bizarre" manner. Roha suddenly stopped breathing shortly after police handcuffed him.
Efforts to revive Roha were unsuccessful and he was declared dead at Foothills Hospital.
The medical examiner conducted an autopsy the next day, however, it wasn't enough to confirm the cause of death.
One of the key factors in the investigation is the toxicology report, which will take at least three weeks to complete, said acting Staff Sgt. Craig Cuthbert of the homicide unit.
The homicide unit's task is to determine if a crime has occurred.
The professional standards section of the city police force is conducting an administrative review of the incident, as required by CPS policy.

Cheryl Hass, manager of the section, said reviews address several questions. Was training an issue? Are policies and procedures adequate? Was there a breach of police service regulations? Are disciplinary measures necessary?

"The review is based on the homicide file, so it's hard to say how long it will take," Hass said. "It depends on the complexity of the case, the number of witnesses. Then the file is sent to Crown counsel."
Crown counsel decides whether criminal charges are warranted.
"It's not uncommon to take up to six months," Hass said.
Family members said Roha had been battling a substance abuse problem for a year. His mother had tried in vain to keep him in treatment.
No drug paraphernalia was found in Roha's motel room, but police said his "erratic" behaviour was consistent with someone who had overdosed.
